name: Aisha Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, political parties or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Cedar House, a family grill restaurant on the high street, always full on weekends. I come in at eleven and thread the skewers, wash and cook the rice, chop the salads, then help on the grill when it gets busy. Mr Farouk, the owner, is a friend of my father's and took me on when nobody else would, because I didn't finish school. I'm still slow with the grill, but I'm careful and I never miss a shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Yusuf, he drives the number twelve bus. We rent a small flat behind the mosque and we'd like a baby next year, God willing. We've got less than a month's money put by. I don't use any of these AI things, I don't see the need, and I don't trust them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I'm glad people can stop panicking. At work I'd say we carry on as we always have. I'm not online much, maybe the family group chat, and I'd say the same there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing gets easier. Yusuf's overtime was cut last spring, prices keep going up, and we want a baby on a cook's pay and a driver's pay. My worry was never computers, it's whether we can afford the family we want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every shift Mr Farouk gives me and ask for Saturday evenings too. I'd cook at home every day, no takeaways, and put a little aside each week for the baby. Maybe I'd ask my mother if she'd mind the baby when it comes so I can keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not frightened, but heavy. Like carrying shopping bags up a hill every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the baby is the main worry. Would you put it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf says wait a year, I say we'll never have enough so why wait. Our grandparents had children with less. But I'd want at least two months saved first, and we have nowhere near that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is Cedar House doing well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekends are full, but weekdays are quieter than before. Mr Farouk's son wants to start doing delivery apps, but the owner says they take too much commission. I think the place is fine, but it's not getting rich.

say: I'd say I'm glad people can **stop panicking**.
I'd say at work and in the family chat we **carry on** as always.
think: My worry is affording the **family we want**, not computers.
My husband's **overtime cut** and rising prices squeeze us already.
do: Work every shift and ask for **Saturday evenings** too.
Cook at home daily and **save weekly** for the baby.
Ask my mother about **minding the baby** so I keep working.
feel: **Heavy**, like carrying shopping bags up a hill every day.
S0.quote: My worry was never computers, it's whether we can afford the family we want.
fieldNote: Aisha's pressure is a **planned baby** on two low incomes.
Her husband's **lost overtime** already hurts the household.
She leans on **family and faith** rather than any public scheme.

steps.text: Ask Mr Farouk for Saturday evening shifts at Cedar House
Cook at home daily and save weekly for the baby
Arrange for her mother to mind the baby while she works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should keep working hard and not wait for the government to save them. At work I'd say nobody's going to replace Cedar House's grill with a computer. In the family chat I'd tell the young ones to learn a trade with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry for Yusuf more than me. The bus company already plans routes with computers. If the bus company starts testing buses with no drivers, my husband's job is the one that goes. My job is chopping and grilling, so I think it lasts a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Yusuf to look at the coach company, the long-distance one, because people still want a driver they can talk to. I'd keep saving whatever I can, maybe twenty a week. I won't touch the AI apps, I'd rather spend my time on work I understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, mostly for him. I'd pray about it more, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Mr Farouk any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's not his business, and he's got his own worries. He's sixty and his son wants to change everything. I'd just keep turning up on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people shouldn't wait for the government. What if Yusuf lost his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the family helps first, that's how we've always done it. My brothers would find him something, maybe at the cash and carry. I'd only go to the government if there was nothing else.

say: I'd say people should **work hard** and not wait for government.
I'd tell the young ones to **learn a trade** with their hands.
think: My husband's **bus job** goes first if they test driverless buses.
My **chopping and grilling** should last a while.
do: Push my husband to apply to the **coach company**.
Stay away from **AI apps** and stick to work I understand.
feel: **Worried for him**, and praying about it more.
S1.quote: If the bus company starts testing buses with no drivers, my husband's job is the one that goes.
fieldNote: Aisha's exposure runs through her **husband's bus job**.
She would turn to **her brothers** before any government help.
Her faith is a **real coping tool**, not a figure of speech.

steps.text: Save twenty a week from her Cedar House wages
Ask her brothers to find Yusuf work at the cash and carry
Keep every shift at Cedar House without changing her routine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, people are made to work, not to sit around while machines do everything. At work I'd say we pray and we keep going. In the family chat I'd say look after your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I don't know what we'd do. The bus company would want robot buses as soon as they're safe, and by 2031 robots could do my grill too. Two jobs, both gone in a few years, a baby maybe on the way, and nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd put the baby off, that's the first thing, which breaks my heart. I'd ask my father if we could move in with them to save the rent. Beyond that, I can't see a plan, I'm not someone who learns new things easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. My chest gets tight just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother about putting off the baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be upset, she wants grandchildren. I'd tell my mother we're waiting until we know we can feed a child. She'd understand, but she'd pray about it loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Cedar House that might last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Farouk says people come for him, for the chat, the welcome. Maybe he keeps one person on the grill for show. But it wouldn't be the junior, it'd be his son.

say: I'd say machines doing everything is **wrong**, because people are made to work.
I'd tell the family chat to **look after your own**.
think: My husband's **bus job** and my grill could both go within a few years.
A **baby on the way** with nothing saved is what frightens me.
do: **Put off the baby**, which breaks my heart.
Ask my father if we can **move in** to save rent.
feel: **Frightened**, with a tight chest just thinking about it.
S2.quote: Two jobs, both gone in a few years, a baby maybe on the way, and nothing saved.
fieldNote: Aisha expects **both household incomes** to vanish within about five years.
She says outright she has **no plan** beyond delaying the baby.
Moving in with her parents is the only **concrete step** she can name.

steps.text: Postpone trying for a baby until the household income is clear
Move into her parents' home to stop paying rent
Ask her father and brothers for help with living costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives families time to prepare, so prepare. At work I'd say don't waste money. In the family chat I'd share advice from the imam about trusting God and working hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's still frightening, but there's time to have the baby first and get them a bit older before the robots come. I've got about eight years before a robot does my grill. Yusuf would have about five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the baby on our plan, next year, and save every spare bit before that. I'd tell Yusuf to get his coach licence in the first two years, because coaches will be last to go driverless. I'd stay at Cedar House and be the most reliable person there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but not drowning. There's a bit of time to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think coaches go driverless last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people on a coach trip want someone to help with the bags and the old people. That's what Yusuf says, anyway. I don't know much about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn anything new yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe baking, from my aunt. My aunt's sweets for weddings and Eid are family knowledge, not a computer course. People will always want those from a real person.

say: I'd say five years gives families **time to prepare**.
I'd share the imam's advice about **trust and hard work**.
think: There's time to **have the baby** before robots come.
I've got about **eight years** before a robot does my grill.
do: Have the baby **next year** as planned and save before then.
Push my husband to get a **coach licence** in two years.
Learn **wedding and Eid sweets** from my aunt.
feel: **Scared**, but with a bit of **time to breathe**.
S3.quote: My aunt's sweets for weddings and Eid are family knowledge, not a computer course.
fieldNote: Aisha still expects to **lose both incomes**, just later.
The extra years mean the **baby stays on plan**.
She looks to **family skills** like her aunt's sweets, not formal courses.

steps.text: Try for a baby next year as planned
Save every spare bit of wages before the baby arrives
Learn to make wedding and Eid sweets from her aunt to sell

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good warning, and families who plan will be fine. At work I'd say keep your head down and keep earning. I'd say the same in the family chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's better. Thirteen years before robots cook means I'm forty, and my child would be at school. I could build up the sweets business slowly and maybe not need the restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the baby, keep working at Cedar House, and start selling sweets for weddings and Eid through the mosque and family. Yusuf would do his coach licence. We'd try to save a few months' money by the time robots come, which would be the first time ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried still, but I can see a way through. Like rain, not a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you sell the sweets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Word of mouth, at the mosque and in the family. My cousin has an online shop, but I'd let her do that part. I'd just make them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, rent and the owner retiring could happen anyway. The robots are just one more thing on the pile.

I'd tell everyone to **keep earning** and keep their heads down.

steps.text: Have the baby next year while keeping her Cedar House job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without question, because Yusuf and I would both lose our work before we'd even had our first child. What would help is proper apprenticeships for adults, paid, so Yusuf could learn a trade. And help for small family places like Cedar House to keep going.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. It's what keeps me steady when I'm scared. I'd rather trust God and my family than wait for a cheque from anyone.

headlineQuote: I'd rather trust God and my family than wait for a cheque from anyone.
portrait: Aisha is a 27-year-old **junior cook** at a family grill restaurant, taken on by a family friend.
She is married to Yusuf, a **bus driver**, and they hope for a baby with little saved.
She is traditional, **never uses AI**, and turns to family and faith before government.
She is **panicked** by fast AGI, expecting both household jobs to go.
With more time, she plans a **sweets business** from family recipes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing both jobs before their first child.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid adult apprenticeships** so her husband can learn a trade.
Support for **small family restaurants** to keep going.
